explains: Every kind of soldier in the realm, in one roster serving both halves of the game. The court reads the top half of each entry (where they come from, how they march, what they owe); the battle reads the bottom half (mass, reach, refusal, traits). Read the counteredBy line first: every unit is beaten by something, always for a reason you can watch happen on the field, never a rule you have to memorise. Levies are OF somewhere — the Spears of Millrow come from Millrow, and losing Millrow removes that named wing from the board, not 'eight percent of your infantry'.

fields.raisedBy: Which holding types (data/holdings.json) or bargains (data/obligations.json) raise this unit.
fields.marchSpeed: Leagues per day on a good summer road.
fields.dailyWear: Fatigue points gained per day on the march.
fields.massPerManKg: Man plus kit — or horse plus man plus kit. Only matters for shock.
fields.drillBase: 0-100 formation quality; the Host's per-unit drill overrides it.
fields.refusalBase: 0-1000. How strongly this unit's set weapons make a charging horse refuse — ONLY when braced, only in the front arc.
fields.refusalRangeMm: How far ahead the refusal reaches. Longer weapons project further.
fields.turnMulPermille: Multiplier on the base turn rate.
fields.fatigueMulPermille: How fast this unit tires, from armour weight and the work.
fields.musterCost: Coin per battle, for the court's arithmetic. Not a battle number.
fields.class: What kind of thing it is — foot, horse, or something that does not fight. It decides which of the engine's speed and fatigue tables the unit is read against.
fields.typicalMen: How many men a unit of this sort usually musters. Real numbers vary with the holding that raised them and how the year has gone.
fields.armour: What they are wearing (see the armour shelf in `data/equipment.json`). Armour reduces wounds rather than hits, and it costs fatigue every minute it is worn.
fields.shield: What they are carrying (see the shields shelf in `data/equipment.json`). Worth a great deal to the front and nothing at all to the rear.
fields.primaryWeapon: What they fight with first (see `data/equipment.json`). Long weapons win the clash and lose the press — the whole Six Seconds inversion is here.
fields.sidearm: What they fall back on once the press starts and there is no room for the long weapon. This is why spearmen have a bad time after six seconds.
fields.missileWeapon: What they shoot with, if anything (see the missile weapons shelf in `data/equipment.json`).
fields.defaultFormation: The shape they take when nobody has said otherwise.
fields.allowedFormations: Every shape they can adopt at all. A unit that cannot form a shieldwall cannot be told to.
fields.traits: The keywords that govern what this unit can do (see `data/keywords.json`). `CanBrace` is the one that decides most battles.
fields.defaultQuirks: Quirks these men carry by their nature rather than by their history (see `data/quirks.json`).
fields.chargeSpeedMmPerTick: How fast they close in the last stretch, overriding the general table. Shock scales with the SQUARE of this, so it is worth far more than it looks.
fields.speedMulPermille: A multiplier on this unit's movement, in thousandths, where it differs from its class.
fields.arrivalReadyTicks: How long after arriving on the field before they are fit to fight. Men who have just marched on are not yet an asset.
fields.steadyRadiusMm: How far this unit's steadiness reaches to hold neighbours together. The quiet reason a household guard is worth more than its own numbers.
fields.signalRadiusMm: How far signals carry from this unit — the banner and the horn reaching the men who need to hear them.
fields.moraleCeilingCap: A hard ceiling on how brave these men can ever get, whatever the court did for them. Fragile men can never be more than two-thirds brave, however well the day is going.

units.name: Militia Spears
units.role: Numbers, quickly, because towns sit on the roads. A crowd in the open field; astonishing behind their own wall.
units.counteredBy: Almost any professional soldier, once their line frays. They will not pursue anybody anywhere.
units.explains: Shopkeepers and apprentices with spears, levied by a town's charter. There are a great many of them and they arrive faster than anyone. Braced and steady they will stop horses like any spear line — the spear does not know who holds it — but their nerve is thin, and a shaken militia brace is mostly decorative, because refusal is multiplied by morale and cohesion.
units.readOnField: A wide, slightly ragged block that gets ragged faster than anyone else's.

units.name: Levy Spearmen
units.role: The backbone of every army you will ever field. Braced, they stop horses. Unbraced, they are men with sticks.
units.counteredBy: Swordsmen once the press starts — their knives are poor. Arrows, because a padded jack is not much. Anything that catches them before they brace.
units.explains: Farmers with a season of training, a spear and a round shield, owed by their manor for forty days a year. Their whole value is BRACING: butt in the earth, point level, and a horse will not come on. Seven metres of refusal is just barely enough to stop a gallop — and it is multiplied by how steady and how neat they are, so frightened fyrdmen with a wobbly line are ridden straight over. When the press comes at six seconds they have a bad time; a spear line wants to hit, hurt, and step back out before then.
units.readOnField: Braced: butts in the earth, points level, absolutely still. Unbraced: shuffling, points wavering.

units.name: Bowmen
units.role: Break the enemy's WILL at two hundred paces, then let somebody else break their bodies.
units.counteredBy: Cavalry that reaches them. Full harness (98 wounds in a thousand). Running out of arrows — they carry thirty-two.
units.explains: Men who have drawn a war bow at the butts every Sunday since boyhood. The bow does not actually kill very many people; being shot at from beyond answer is UNBEARABLE, and unbearable is what routs armies — so the right use of archers is never 'kill them with arrows', it is 'make them breakable, then charge'. Two things make bowmen more than a nuisance: STAKES — ninety seconds of hammering buys a hedge of points nearly as good as pikes, and unlike pikemen the archers keep shooting — and the MAUL, the stake-hammer that also flattens an exhausted man in plate. Bowmen finishing knights is arithmetic, not legend.
units.readOnField: Loose spacing you can count from across the field; volleys that arc for three seconds and land together; a visible fence of stakes.

units.name: Foresters
units.role: The best value in the game — in the trees. The worst — in a line.
units.counteredBy: Cavalry in the open, absolutely and always. Being cornered against anything.
units.explains: People who eat because they can hit a moving deer. Superb shots, quick on their feet, slow to tire — and constitutionally unable to stand in a formed line where somebody can hit them back, which they know perfectly well and so should you. On the SCREEN job they back away automatically from anything that comes within forty-five paces, so they work without a single order. In woodland, where formations cannot hold and arrows are half wasted, they are the most dangerous troops on the field.
units.readOnField: Scattered, constantly moving, always backing away. If they are standing still in the open, something has gone wrong.

units.name: Pick-men
units.role: What a rich mine gives you instead of soldiers.
units.counteredBy: Everything — and above all anything that frightens them, because they will be the first thing on your side to run.
units.explains: Miners with picks and hammers. Strong arms, heavy iron — their blows actually go through armour better than a swordsman's — and no idea what they are doing, no armour of their own, and a courage ceiling two-thirds of anyone else's. Their real use is digging under walls. On a battlefield, stand them somewhere quiet and far from anything you love, because when they break they will take the heart of everyone within ninety paces with them.
units.readOnField: A shapeless block that flinches visibly under fire.

units.name: Men-at-Arms
units.role: The grinder. Put them where the fight will be longest and let them win it slowly.
units.counteredBy: Their own wind — harness burns half again the fatigue of anyone else, and a blown man in armour cannot lift his arms. Mud. Crossbows and mauls. And being made to chase skirmishers, which is the actual historical answer.
units.explains: Professional soldiers of a castle household, head to foot in steel, with poleaxes. You cannot cut them: a sword lands thirty-eight wounds in a thousand on full harness. You can barely shoot them. What you CAN do is make them run: their armour costs wind half again as fast as anyone's, and a tired unit swings slower, moves slower, and permanently loses morale ceiling. Never fight them; tire them.
units.readOnField: Slow, glittering, pushing through everything. Later: the same block, stopped, breathing.

units.name: Crossbowmen
units.role: The answer to armour. Twenty-four bolts that go through anything.
units.counteredBy: Everything fast. They shoot a third as often as a war bow and are useless the moment they must move.
units.explains: Guildsmen with steel-bowed crossbows and standing shields. A crossbow takes an afternoon to learn and puts a bolt through full harness two hundred and fifty-nine times in a thousand — near three times what a war bow manages. The trade is rate: a volley every long while, and the pavise shelters them from the front ONLY while they stand still. Castles raise the better sort; towns the cheaper — same trade, different quality, which is the muster's business, not this sheet's.
units.readOnField: Big shields planted in a line, men crouched behind them winding cranks. When the shields come down, they are running.

units.name: Marines
units.role: The line that does not move — and does not die when the press comes. Spear at reach, sword in the crush.
units.counteredBy: Being flanked; the kite shield covers one direction. Poleaxes and mauls through the mail. Being made to chase anybody.
units.explains: Dock-fighters and boarding parties off a port's ships, used to the most confined and vicious fighting there is. They matter because they carry a SWORD as well as a spear: for the first six seconds they fight at reach like spearmen, and when the press comes and the spear becomes a fence post they draw steel and keep winning. Almost nothing else on foot is good in BOTH halves of a melee — the manual's whole lesson about sidearms, standing in one unit.
units.readOnField: Overlapping shields, a very straight line, and a visible moment when the shafts drop and the swords come out.

units.name: Knights
units.role: One enormous hammer blow, delivered to the right place at the right speed. Then reform, then again.
units.counteredBy: Braced points, absolutely. Mud, which halves charge speed and so quarters shock. Charging from too close, which is your fault. And archers, because a horse is a very large target.
units.explains: Armoured men on armoured horses, going nine metres a second. At full gallop into unbraced men they kill by the dozen in the first instant; into braced pikes they kill a tenth of a man, because the points take the SPEED away and shock is the square of the speed. And the thing nobody expects: charging home disorders the CHARGER — a knight unit that strikes loses two hundred thousand cohesion and needs twenty seconds standing to redress. Cavalry is a piston: charge, strike, wheel out, reform, charge — and every stroke costs a rider out and a rider back, so how many pistons you can run at once IS your courier count, which is a court number. That is where the politics touches the field hardest. They are also your proudest vassals and worth ransoms, both of which will cost you.
units.readOnField: Lances level at forty paces. The last five seconds tell the whole story: still accelerating means somebody dies; slowing means the brace held.

units.name: March Riders
units.role: Get round the side. Sting and be gone. Chase the broken. Pretend to run away.
units.counteredBy: Anything that catches them and can hit them — their armour is light and their ponies bare.
units.explains: Frontier horsemen who have been raiding and being raided since childhood, on quick ponies, with javelins they throw at a canter. They turn nearly four times as fast as a pike block, so they win every race to a flank; they can shoot while moving, so they never have to accept a fight; and they carry the Feigner's craft — the false retreat that pulls a hothead out of his line and onto your knights. When an enemy breaks, nobody reaps a rout like march riders: mounted pursuers kill three and a half times faster and catch twice the ransoms.
units.readOnField: Loose, fast, always at the edges of the picture. When they turn and come back at somebody who chased them, that is the trap closing.

units.name: Household Guard
units.role: The steadiest men on any field you will fight on, and the only ones who do exactly what they are told the first time.
units.counteredBy: Nothing in particular and numbers in general. There are never enough of them, because every crown they cost is a crown not settling a grudge.
units.explains: Your own paid soldiers, who live where you live. No letters, no waiting, no excuses, no grudges — the obedience number on this contingent is the highest in the game, which you will feel every time an order lands. They cost three crowns a man every season whether there is a war or not, and that arithmetic is the whole reason the rest of the feudal system exists.
units.readOnField: Dressed ranks that stay dressed. The block the rest of the line secretly watches.

units.name: Sworn Brothers
units.role: Sixty men who will not run away from anything, ever, for free — and are not entirely yours.
units.counteredBy: Their own certainty. A unit that cannot retreat is a unit that can be destroyed in place, and their obedience can never rise above 55.
units.explains: Warrior monks of the Sworn Order, housed in an abbey's chapter, who come only for a cause your Chaplain has blessed. The best-drilled foot in the game, they do not flee — which is not always good news — and they answer their own Grandmaster before your Marshal, so at some point they will do what they believe is right instead of what you asked. Resolve like iron and obedience capped at 55 is a very specific kind of nightmare to command.
units.readOnField: A block that advances when the horn says advance and, occasionally, when God does.

units.name: Free Company Swords
units.role: Get inside the points and win the press. This unit exists to punish spears and pikes.
units.counteredBy: The first six seconds of anything with reach. Cavalry, always. Arrows in the open.
units.explains: Hired men in mail with swords and small shields, and exactly one plan: survive the reach and win the crush. Against a pike hedge they lose badly for six seconds and then win overwhelmingly for the next sixty, because in the press long weapons drop to one fighting rank and take their crowd penalty while a sword takes none. They are professionals in three countries' wars — and they are mercenaries: run up arrears and their courage has no floor and their loyalty has a price the enemy can also pay.
units.readOnField: Close, quick, shoulder-to-shoulder work, and a visible turn in the fight at the six-second mark.

units.name: Free Company Pikes
units.role: A wall that horses cannot cross. Nothing else in the game stops a charge as completely.
units.counteredBy: Its own flanks — brace is front-arc only and it turns at half speed, so a quarter-wheel takes eight and a half seconds. Arrows, because it is dense and unshielded. And swordsmen who get inside the points.
units.explains: Two hundred drilled mercenaries, eight ranks deep, with pikes longer than four men are tall. Braced, the hedge projects twelve metres of refusal — horses stop dead, and the shock of a charge falls by a factor of hundreds, because shock is the square of the speed the points took away. Then the pikes kill the stalled horses at leisure. But: refusal is only to the front; the block turns slower than anything on the field; it has nothing but belt-knives when the press comes, and dies in it sixteen to one; and it is the densest arrow target that has ever stood still. A pike hedge is a wall, and walls do not manoeuvre.
units.readOnField: A forest of shafts at head height. Its failure is equally unmistakable: the shafts go vertical and the block folds inward.

units.name: Free Company Horse
units.role: Knights you can rent. Two-thirds of the punch at half the price and none of the pride — as long as the pay chest is full.
units.counteredBy: The same physics that beats knights, only sooner — and an empty treasury, which beats them completely.
units.explains: Professional horsemen who serve the purse. At 380 a tick their shock is about seven-tenths of a knight's — the square again — and their horses are unarmoured, which shows badly under arrows. They carry the game's most brutal wire between treasury and field: with arrears unpaid, every couple of seconds there is a small chance they simply ride off the field. Not a morale penalty. They go home.
units.readOnField: Good horse doing sound work — or, if you did not pay them, an empty place where good horse used to be.

units.name: The Crown Banner
units.role: The commander's voice, made of cloth and forty picked men. There is no other body on the field that is you.
units.counteredBy: Being taken. That is the whole point of it existing.
units.explains: There is no player character in this game. There is a banner, and the picked men around it, and that is where your voice comes from. While it stands, every unit that can SEE it takes your orders in one second instead of a nine-second ride, and every friend within a hundred paces is steadied. If it falls, every unit in the army loses a quarter of its will at once and your signal range goes to nothing — every order forever after is a courier. Put it forward and your voice carries; put it forward and it can be reached. Where you plant it says what you believe.
units.readOnField: The tallest thing on the field. If it goes down you will not need to be told.

units.name: Relic Bearers
units.role: A courage engine that cannot defend itself.
units.counteredBy: One troop of light horse that nobody was watching.
units.explains: Clerics carrying a saint's bones on a bier, who march only when the cause is blessed. They cannot fight at all. Within a hundred and twenty paces they steady everyone; once a battle, they may absolve one contingent — a great surge of heart, free, no rider needed. If the relic is captured, the whole army's will takes a wound and so does the crown's standing with the Church, into next season. Bringing the saint to the field is a court decision with a battlefield price — the shape of the whole game in one unit.
units.readOnField: A slow, tottering knot of unarmed men with a gilt box, always somewhere they should not be.

units.name: The Bombard
units.role: Terror at three hundred paces, twice a minute.
units.counteredBy: Walking twenty paces to the left. Also its own gunpowder.
units.explains: A hooped iron tube on a sledge that throws a stone the size of a man's chest at roughly the right part of the field. It kills almost nobody — but its fear multiplier is near three times a war bow's, and fear is what actually decides battles. It moves at a seventh of walking pace, so wherever you put it at the start is where it is; and one shot in sixteen bursts the tube and kills the crew. A bad investment that everyone wants, which is exactly right.
units.readOnField: One enormous noise, a furrow ploughed through a formation, and the whole enemy line flinching at once.
